newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda to present coffee stabilisation proposals.
newsitem.headline: Uganda to present coffee stabilisation proposals.

text.p: Uganda will present proposals to stabilise the coffee market at a London producer meeting this week while Ugandan leaders were urging roasters in overseas markets to turn to robustas.

The Uganda Coffee Development Authority would not say what the proposals were. But authorities in Uganda were excited that the current market situation gave them an opportunity to boost the standing of their robustas.
Uganda is among countries that have already agreed to hold on to some of their available coffee to keep prices stable.
Coffee producers are holding two days of talks in London this week against a backdrop of a surge in coffee prices which took U.S. arabica futures to a 20-year high last week.

Uganda Coffee Trade Federation (UCTF) president Paul Mugambwa, saying that Uganda's robustas were rated as among the best in the world because of their mildness and aroma, said Uganda was prepared to meet any demand by a switch to robustas.
"If there's an expected increase in demand, Uganda is very prepared to address it," Mugambwa told Reuters.
Federation Executive Director Frederick Kawuma also said Uganda would offer the best quality robustas and called roasters to take advantage of the situation and buy Uganda's coffee.
"Uganda is happy to offer the best robustas in the world so the traders will respond to what the roasters want," he said.

But other industry leaders said it was not possible for roasters to switch to robustas but they could significantly increase the amounts of robustas in their blends. However they said that would, in fact, be only temporary.
"There's a limit in the blending which cannot exceed 50 percen,t as end-consumers would detect change and possibly reduce their consumption," one senior coffee analyst said.
"The increase is not indefinite. They (roasters) will reach a saturation point when they cannot increase anymore so this will not go on for too long," added the Kampala-based analyst.
The analyst said that overall retail prices were rising because of rising cost of production and rising arabicas.
Rising coffee prices in recent months have affected consumption in the United States and Germany.
"We're in a critical period," a Ugandan coffee trader said.
The trader said coffee supply from Brazil, Colombia and Mexico was expected to be lower than average in 1996/97 and 1997/98.
"That indicates a very bad situation," the trader said.
Ugandan coffee experts were concerned that the gap in price between arabicas and robustas would continue to widen.
Uganda will export around 3.9 million bags of coffee in 1996/97 compared to around 4.2 million bags in 1995/96. That is lower than previous forecasts of up to 4.4 million bags.

So far, cumulative coffee exports during the first seven months of 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) increased by 8.9 percent compared to last season -- totalling 2,944,168 bags compared to 2,703,507 bags in the same period last year.
Coffee is Uganda's predominant foreign exchange earner.
Some 88 percent of Uganda's coffee is robusta while only 12 percent is of the premium arabica variety.
